brief.head: Brains, not stomachs
brief.text: Amit Varma rejects overpopulation outright. People move from sparse places to dense, prosperous cities, voting with their feet, and they are minds that create value, not mouths. {050-C01}

brief.head: A ₹300 helper
brief.text: Asked for something under ₹10,000, Ajay Shah chose a ₹300 pill case. He fills it once a week, then obeys it like a zombie, no longer missing doses. {#pillcase}

brief.head: Money follows child
brief.text: Large parts of India have left state schools for private ones, Ajay Shah said. Public money should follow the child, through vouchers, not reward only state-school pupils. {050-C05}

brief.head: One person, one vote
brief.text: Restrict voting to those who pass a test? Amit Varma said no: “the moment you create a bar, somebody decides what that bar is.” {050-C30}

brief.head: Kinky development
brief.text: Borrowing Lant Pritchett’s distinction, Amit Varma contrasted national development, ending poverty, with “kinky development”: small, neat questions that advance careers. RCTs, he said, are the classic example. {050-C16}

thought.text: Stop daydreaming. Pick one. Immerse yourself in it. Love the doing of it.
thought.who: Amit Varma, to young people paralysed by possibilities, and to his younger self

lead.kicker: At episode 50, Amit Varma and Ajay Shah take questions
lead.head: Fifty up, and no holds barred
body: For its fiftieth episode, *Everything is Everything* turned the floor over to its listeners. They sent questions on Twitter and elsewhere, Ajay Shah sorted and shortened them, and Amit Varma, for once, needed no notes.
The hosts had also moved. They had come to Bir, in Himachal Pradesh, for a week, to record ten episodes they are calling the Bir sessions. {#bir}
Shah arrived at the end of a hike, his first big outing after a fracture in January.
With so many questions, Shah warned, the answers would be “like helicopter tours”. They ranged from blood and water to Bob Dylan, from the central bank to crying at films.
## The case for growth
Two convictions ran under the tour. The first was that growth is the answer to poverty, and that the Indian state has often stood in its way.
Asked why India lost the garment trade to Bangladesh, Shah said only about 35 per cent of working-age Indians are employed, among the worst rates in the world. {#employment}

Idle workers should bring wages down. Instead, he said, high minimum wages and dense labour laws make big workforces “dangerous and difficult” to hire, so firms stay small and the factories go to Bangladesh.

Degrowth got short shrift. “For a country at the poverty levels of India, degrowth is just morally wrong,” Shah said. {050-C04} Varma called it a classic luxury belief, held by the rich from air-conditioned rooms.
## The trouble with the state

The second conviction was scepticism of the state as it actually works. Most Indian state bodies, Shah said, are not institutions but personalised organisations, which change with whoever runs them. {050-C07}

The hosts’ one real disagreement came here. Shah often justifies state action by pointing to market failure; Varma thinks market failure rare and government failure everywhere. Their values, Varma said, are fully aligned.

Shah owned up to a change of mind. He once believed Moore’s Law, Unix and the internet would make the world better. Now he thinks they add magnitude to whatever people already are, for good or for ill. {050-C21}
Varma, more optimistic about technology and AI, called it a net positive.
## Living well

The other half of the questions were about life, and here the answers grew smaller in scale. Shah’s advice to the young was to drop two habits: competing with others, and living life as a performance.
Varma recalled a café in Bir the day before, where he asked everyone when they were happiest. In the mountains, said one. With her dog, said another. When he has a new idea, said Shah.
Every answer, Varma noticed, was easy to reach. People who define happiness by grand goals, he said, are chasing something elusive.
Not everything was serene. Varma admitted he wastes hours on bullet chess, and wishes he had never thought himself intelligent as a young man.
Shah, offered a genie, would send a bag of books back to the leaders of 1947.
Then the hosts thanked their listeners. This was not two people talking in a vacuum, Varma said: “we’re having a conversation with each other, but also in a sense with you.”
Shah had tried to end it earlier: “Amit, I’m starving.” Varma stopped him to say goodbye to the listeners first, then asked: “Should we go for lunch?”

second.label: Crisis management
second.head: Cliffhanger, solved
second.deck: Amit Varma tells how Ajay Shah broke his leg, and kept his head
body: Asked whether he is ever irrational and emotional, Ajay Shah said he is. But he does not rattle easily, and he has a rule for crises: “the bigger the crisis, the more calm and collected you need to be”. {#crisis}
Amit Varma had a story to prove it. On a hike, for the first time in 30 years or so, Shah had an accident: he fell off the edge of what appeared to be a mountain and was left hanging. {#thirtyyears}

His friend Ayush grabbed his hand. Shah was so panicked that his body was covered in sweat. For about thirty seconds Ayush held him, and not a word passed between them. Then Shah looked up and said: “Let’s solve this.” {050-S08}

quote.text: And then Ajay looked up at Ayush and said, Let’s solve this. So that’s Ajay Shah for you.

second.caption: the day Ajay Shah broke his leg

third.head: Mask on, reflux off
body: A listener asked Amit Varma about sleep apnoea. His advice: if you snore, get tested. He thought something like 20 per cent of people have the problem. {#apnea}
It stops your breathing in sleep, so you wake without realising and are tired by day. Obesity, an issue for him, can cause it.

Varma tested positive for a mild case and took to a CPAP machine. It transformed his life in an unexpected way. Sleep had never been his trouble. Acid reflux had: for years he woke with a cold or a sore throat.

The air gushing in through a nasal mask, he found, keeps the acid down. The morning sore throats stopped. {050-S02} Still, he would not tell everyone with reflux to buy one: “I don’t really know what to make of it.”
third.caption: his CPAP machine

p2.title: Asked and answered
p2.deck: From the creator economy to caste, the arguments behind Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s rapid-fire answers

sections.label: Making a living
sections.head: Reach first, revenue later
sections.caption: reach and revenue
body: Rishav Datta asked Amit Varma what he does for a living. “I’m a professional podcaster as of now,” Varma said. Ajay Shah offered a gloss: “you’re just giving gifts to the universe.”

Varma thinks of the creator economy in terms of two Rs, reach and revenue. {050-C09} The podcast gives him reach, reach builds credibility, and revenue comes from somewhere. Much of it was, and is, his writing course, the Art of Clear Writing, which he said has had some 2,500 students. {#students}
Early students came because of his podcast and blog; now they come by word of mouth. But whatever you do, for reach or revenue, he said, you have to put your heart and soul into it.
## Own your readers

Asked how to build a career in long-form journalism, Varma was frank. India lacks outlets like *The New Yorker* or *The Atlantic*, and beat reporters have vanished. In his friend Prem Panicker’s words, journalism ends up “a mile wide and an inch deep”. {050-J11}

His advice to any writer is to start a newsletter. Wait for newspapers and you write rarely, within word counts and news cycles, with your readers scattered. “That email database belongs to you,” he said, “not to a Substack or to any other newsletter site.” {050-C10}
~ Doing what he loves without compromise, he said, took decades. The shows remain a labour of love: he doubts he is net positive from them in money. {#netpositive}

quote.text: You have to think of what you do in terms of two Rs. One is reach and one is revenue.

sections.label: The economy
sections.head: Stitched up by the state
sections.caption: India’s lost garment trade
body: Why did India lose the garment trade to Bangladesh? Ajay Shah began with a number: only about 35 per cent of working-age Indians are employed, among the worst rates anywhere. {#employment}

So many idle hands should drive wages down. Instead, high minimum wages and labour laws deter big workforces. In Bangladesh, he said, the minimum wage is 8,000, “so people get jobs”, and firms from all over the world build factories there. {#eastbengal}
Amit Varma spelt out the arithmetic. Set a minimum wage of ₹15,000, and a worker who would have had a job at ₹12,000 does not get one at all. {#minwage} It hurts “the poorest of the poor”.
## Grow first
Degrowth, Shah said, is morally wrong for a country as poor as India, whose income per person, adjusted for purchasing power, is about a tenth of America’s. {050-C04}

He sorted capitalism’s ills by cause. Low wages and poor conditions yield to growth: the poorest factory is hot, a richer one gets fans, a richer one still is air-conditioned. Pollution is an externality, to be met with taxes, Coasean bargains or the state.

~ Varma called degrowth a luxury belief, and pointed to Bjorn Lomborg’s *The Skeptical Environmentalist*: London, a century ago, was polluted and unhealthy, and cleaned up as it grew prosperous. {050-R10}

quote.text: So India has a self-inflicted wound of an artificially low working population and artificially small economy

sections.label: Learning
sections.head: Right book, right moment
sections.caption: the right book at the right time
body: Five listeners asked, in one form or another, how the hosts know so much. Amit Varma started with distraction. His phone greys out Twitter and Instagram after half an hour a day each.

Then read, take notes, and bookmark the best minds on Twitter, filing the bookmarks in folders to revisit. “You play Candy Crush for an hour, your future self is stupider,” he said; read for an hour and you make your future self smarter. {050-C12}

Ajay Shah added purpose. Chase a job or fame and you may get it, and then what? “Life is too long to run on such middle level goals.” {050-C13} He also urged investing in your “five, fifteen, fifty people”, and learning by adjacencies.
## The matching process
Shah doubts there is an objectively great book. We change through time, so the trick is to engage lightly with many and keep a mental index, until the right one arrives at the right time. {050-C11}

Two of his came from Lant Pritchett: *Seeing Like a State* and *The Functions of the Executive*, a 1938 management book. His moral: “gentle reader, hang out with people who know great books.” {050-S05}
~ Learning India, he said, is not like learning physics. Look out of the window, and notice how the gender mix of flights changes with the time of day. {050-C14}

quote.text: And what we need is the matching process where the right book shows up at the right time.

sections.label: The state
sections.head: People go, the rules stay
sections.caption: institutions and organisations
body: In India, Ajay Shah said, the word “institution” is bandied about too loosely. An institution is an impersonal capability: people come and go, but it behaves in a predictable and consistent way. {050-C07}

Hindustan Lever, where CEOs come and go, qualifies. Most Indian state bodies do not: they are personalised organisations. For RBI to emerge as an institution, he said, India needed the legal changes for inflation targeting.

Why accept a central bank fixing the short-term interest rate? Shah answered from first principles: money solves the double coincidence of wants, and “the only recipe we know to make money involves the central bank picking a number for the interest rate at the short end”. {050-C06}
## Unlucky in 1947

Given a genie’s wish, Shah would revisit 1947, an unlucky year. India’s founders were formed between 1927 and 1947, when freedom did badly worldwide and war economies made total state mobilisation normal. {050-C27}

He would take Nehru, Gandhi, Rajagopalachari and others a bag of books. The new state, he said, should have spent about 10 per cent of GDP on basics: rule of law, the judiciary, a tax system with rule of law.
~ Amit Varma doubted that books alone would have changed minds formed over decades. Shah’s own conversion by *Seeing Like a State*, he said, came at the right time.

quote.text: I feel that we just got very, very unlucky in the great freedom movement generation, where I think 1947 was an unlucky year.

sections.label: Freedom
sections.head: No Ram Rajya on offer
sections.caption: spontaneous order and its ills
body: A listener pressed the point: patriarchy, caste and global warming are products of spontaneous order too. Ajay Shah’s first answer was to drop utopia. “There will be no Ram Rajya.” {050-J17}

Global warming, he said, is a market failure that calls for state action. Social evils must change from the bottom up, because what is imposed from the top may not work and is “truly dangerous because who knows what the values and the culture of the people at the top are”. {050-C15}

Amit Varma called spontaneous order a description, not a verdict. The world still has sexism, he said, but it is much better for women than a century ago, through markets and changing values rather than the lazy call for another law.
## Markets against caste

On caste, Varma drew on Tony Joseph and David Reich: some 2,000 years of enforced caste endogamy made India a collection of small, closed populations, shrinking networks and breeding diseases found nowhere else. {050-C28}

His remedy echoes the Dalit scholar Chandra Bhan Prasad, whose two heroes are Babasaheb Ambedkar and Adam Smith: growth and cities. When firms compete for workers and customers, discrimination gets costly.
~ This is also where the hosts part ways, a little. Shah often invokes market failure; Varma thinks it rare. “Government failure is ubiquitous,” he said. {050-C19}

quote.text: If you’re looking for a large population, look at the Han Chinese. But India is really a collection of thousands of small populations.
quote.who: David Reich, as quoted by Amit Varma

sections.label: How to live
sections.head: Drop the race, skip the show
sections.caption: competition and performance
body: How should a young person find meaning? Ajay Shah’s answer was to stop two things: competing to outdo classmates and neighbours, and living “life as a performance” for social media or the résumé. {050-C24}
Drop both, he said, and what is left is the stuff you value. The same habits, he thinks, are why he does not rattle easily.

Amit Varma urged thought before marrying or having children: is it what you want, or René Girard’s mimetic desire, wanting what others want? Choose communities by values, not circumstance. His own lament: “I am cosmopolitan but I’m not rooted enough.” {050-C23}
## The best at time T
Varma’s new rule is to end each year fitter and with more done. Shah demurred: ageing happens “with probability one”. Better to aim to be “the best Amit Varma I can be at time T”. {050-C26}

For young people paralysed by options, Varma offered Steve Jobs’s advice to Jony Ive: learn to say no to things you love, then commit to one. {050-C25} Shah added: apprentice yourself to a passionate master.
~ Varma closed with Richard Bach: “What a caterpillar calls the end of the world, the master calls a butterfly.” {050-J15}

quote.text: How you spend your days, of course, is how you spend your life.
quote.who: Annie Dillard, as quoted by Amit Varma

side.boxText: Listeners sent questions on Twitter and elsewhere. Ajay Shah collated and paraphrased them, and apologised for any lost nuance. The episode opened the Bir sessions: a week in Himachal Pradesh, ten episodes recorded. {#bir}

contQuote.text: And if there was good values and good character inside you, then the CPUs and the internet have taken that vector and added magnitude to that vector.

stories.caption: his shirts
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on khadi, Udaipur and a wardrobe of gifts
stories.head: From khadi white to silk prints
body: A whole group of listeners had questions about Ajay Shah’s shirts. Mayank asked whether he buys them or is given them. Arpita asked how he chooses them, for normal life and for the show. Eric Paul just wanted to know where to get them. {#shirts}

For years, Shah said, he wore a uniform “stolen from the look” of the economists Kirit Parikh and Shekhar Shah: a plain white or off-white shirt from Khadi Emporium, every single day of the year. {#uniform}

The sleeves were half, because India is too hot for full sleeves, and it took him years to gain the confidence to give up full-sleeved shirts. He has worn a suit and tie abroad, he said, but never in his whole life in India.
Then, many years later, he stumbled on printed shirts. He thinks it was at Udaipur. He bought a few, and it was “an interesting different look”.

Around then the hosts got going on *Everything is Everything*, and Shah thought: why not experiment? He wore some of the printed shirts on the show, and they looked good. He bought more, and people began giving them to him. “Most of my shirts are actually gifts.” {050-S10}
A couple come from an Arvind retail outlet in Ahmedabad, and some came by mail order. Several are silk shirts from Indian Colours, printed with contemporary Indian art.
~ He said he could give people a list of the sources.
stories.why: A borrowed uniform gave way, late and almost by accident, to a signature look. Conventions can be dropped at any age: the show became the place to experiment, and most of what followed arrived as gifts. {050-S10}

stories.start: So I'll go to Delhi, I'll record eight episodes in nine days
stories.end: It's an ongoing battle with discipline and our own minds.
stories.caption: working from Starbucks
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the battle with his own attention
stories.head: Sheepish in a coffee shop
body: Amit Varma banks episodes. He will go to Delhi and record eight episodes of *The Seen and the Unseen* in nine days, do the same in Bangalore, then have weeks free. {#bank}
Balance, he said, is not his problem. Waste is. In the hours he sets aside for work, he gets distracted and plays online bullet chess for hours.

He has built a home office he loves, sit-stand desk and all. He still goes to Starbucks to work, because sitting there with a laptop, “you feel a little sheepish about playing chess for an hour.” {050-S03}
~ “I struggle as much as you do,” he told listeners. “It’s an ongoing battle with discipline and our own minds.”
stories.why: Discipline is often a matter of where you sit rather than how hard you try. And the people who seem most productive, Varma admitted, are fighting the same battle as everyone else.
stories.postscript: His Chess.com bullet rating, he said, rises about 100 points on keto or modafinil days, and falls back when he stops. {050-S04}

stories.start: Like when I did my episode with Vinne, he grew up in a village
stories.end: it's untapped and there is so much hunger for knowledge and entertainment in that
stories.caption: Vinay Singhal’s two languages
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Vinay Singhal and the future of dialects
stories.head: A thousand true fans for Haryanvi
body: Vinay Singhal grew up in a Haryana village, Amit Varma recalled from his episode with him, and twice in his life he had to try really hard.
The first time was when he joined an English-medium school in the eighth standard. He didn’t know English properly, worked at it and reached the top of his class. {#vinay}
The second came when he moved to a city, probably Delhi, Varma thought. Now the problem was Hindi: at home he had spoken Haryanvi. That is the great flattening, as dialects give way in towns.
~ Yet Singhal’s venture, STAGE, makes content in Haryanvi, Bhojpuri and Maithili. Online, the long tail survives, because “every dialect will at least have a thousand true fans”. {050-S07}
stories.why: Two forces pull on India’s languages: a flattening towards Hindi and English, and an internet that rewards niches. Varma’s advice to new podcasters follows: if your other language is nearly as good as your English, use it.
stories.postscript: His hope: that the great flattening becomes “a mere echo from the past”.

stories.start: There is six liters of blood in the average human body.
stories.end: They're being overcautious and drinking too much. So something to watch out for.
stories.caption: dehydration and the heart
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on six litres of blood and a training trick
stories.head: Thin on water, thick in blood
body: An average human body holds six litres of blood, Ajay Shah said. Sweat out a litre and you lose 16.66 per cent of it, which is material. The blood thickens, and the heart works harder. {050-S01}

That is why dehydrated exercise feels so tiring, and why water brings relief. Shah’s twist: on a treadmill, with a fridge of water nearby, you could deliberately train short of water to push your heart harder.
Amit Varma saw an opening. “The Bengali in me is freaking delighted,” he said: he could stay away from water, walk around gently, and still work his heart. {050-J01}
~ Then he turned serious. Having once read some twenty to forty running books in a couple of months, he warned that in marathons a lot of people die from drinking too much.

quote.text: So the blood becomes thicker. When the blood is thicker, it is harder for the heart to pump that blood.

quiz.q: What share of working-age Indians did Ajay Shah say are employed, and how does that rank?
quiz.a: About 35 per cent, among the worst employment rates in the world.

quiz.q: What unexpected ailment did Amit Varma’s CPAP machine cure, after he began using it for sleep apnoea?
quiz.a: His chronic acid reflux, and the morning colds and sore throats it caused.

quiz.q: What distinguishes an institution from a mere organisation, in Ajay Shah’s definition?
quiz.a: It works predictably and consistently, whoever comes and goes: an impersonal capability.

quiz.q: Which phrase did Amit Varma borrow from Lant Pritchett to describe small questions that advance careers?
quiz.a: Kinky development, as opposed to national development, with RCTs the classic example.

quiz.q: Whose look did Ajay Shah’s old uniform of plain white khadi shirts copy?
quiz.a: The economists Kirit Parikh and Shekhar Shah: Khadi Emporium shirts, half-sleeved.

quiz.q: Which law explains, for Ajay Shah, why Indian parents push their children towards English?
quiz.a: Metcalfe’s law: a network’s value grows with the square of its nodes.
